docs.title: Reactify
docs.text: 🫧 Metaball-style "gooey" UI for Compose Multiplatform: blobs that merge, stretch a neck, and pinch apart as items animate from a source into a target.

docs.title: What is this?
docs.text:
Reactify renders a frame as a GooeyScene: a list of blobs (round rects, circles, capsules) that smoothly merge via a polynomial smooth-min, plus cutouts that smoothly subtract. On top of that SDF core it builds three ready-to-use pieces:

  • Transfer — drag or tap an item in a list and watch a token fly into a card, with a gooey bridge connecting the two while it travels.
  • Notch shape — a rounded rect with a concave notch that opens/closes in sync with a transfer target, built from the same distance field.
  • Sliding indicators — a liquid pill that bridges between a bottom-nav item or a segmented control option as the selection changes.

Rendering is pluggable: AGSL (RuntimeShader) on Android API 33+, SkSL via Skiko on iOS, or a CPU path-tracing fallback everywhere else — pick automatically with GooeyRenderers.auto().

Head to Getting Started to add it to your project.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
All notable changes to this project are documented in this file.

The format is based on Keep a Changelog, and this project adheres to Semantic Versioning.

docs.title: 0.1.0-alpha01 - 2026-10-14
docs.text: Initial release.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• GooeyScene core: blobs (round rects, circles, capsules) that merge via a polynomial smooth-min, plus cutouts that smoothly subtract.
  • Transfer — GooeyTransferHost, GooeySource, GooeyTarget: tap or long-press-drag an item into a target, with a gooey bridge connecting the two while it travels.
  • Bottom nav indicator — GooeyNavIndicatorHost, Modifier.gooeyNavItem: a liquid pill that bridges between bottom-nav items as the selection changes.
  • Segmented control — GooeySegmentedControlHost: the same liquid-pill behavior for a segmented control.
  • GooeyNotchShape, a rounded rect with a concave notch that opens/closes in sync with a transfer target.
  • Pluggable rendering via GooeyRenderers: AGSL (RuntimeShader) on Android API 33+, SkSL via Skiko on iOS, and a CPU path-tracing fallback (GooeyRenderers.path()) everywhere else, with GooeyRenderers.auto() picking the best one for the platform. GooeyRenderers.plain() draws blobs without merging, for debugging layouts. See Choosing a Renderer.
  • Kotlin Multiplatform support (Android + iOS), with shared sample screens in samples-shared.
  • Published to Maven Central as io.github.veroanggraa:reactify.
  • MkDocs documentation site, published at veroanggraa.github.io/Reactify.
  • Sample app (app for Android, iosApp for iOS) demoing an invite-friends list, bottom-nav indicator, and segmented control.

docs.title: Including in your project
docs.text:
// Compose Multiplatform (Android + iOS)
kotlin {
    sourceSets {
        commonMain.dependencies {
            implementation("io.github.veroanggraa:reactify:0.1.0-alpha01")
        }
    }
}

// Android only
dependencies {
    implementation("io.github.veroanggraa:reactify:0.1.0-alpha01")
}

Supported targets: android, iosArm64, iosSimulatorArm64, iosX64.

docs.title: Bottom Navigation Indicator
docs.text:
AndroidiOS

A liquid pill that bridges between bottom-nav items as the selection changes. It wraps any NavigationBar (or your own row of tabs) — you only add one Modifier and one state object.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
This snippet is self-contained; paste it into a @Composable screen and it runs as-is.

import androidx.compose.foundation.layout.fillMaxWidth
import androidx.compose.material3.NavigationBar
import androidx.compose.material3.NavigationBarItem
import androidx.compose.material3.NavigationBarItemDefaults
import androidx.compose.material3.Text
import androidx.compose.ui.graphics.Color
import com.veroanggra.reactify.navbar.GooeyNavIndicatorHost
import com.veroanggra.reactify.navbar.gooeyNavItem
import com.veroanggra.reactify.navbar.rememberGooeyNavIndicatorState

private data class Tab(val label: String, val color: Color)

private val tabs = listOf(
    Tab("Home", Color(0xFFC8F5D4)),
    Tab("Search", Color(0xFFC4E4F7)),
    Tab("Chat", Color(0xFFFFF1B8)),
    Tab("Profile", Color(0xFFF6C6CC)),
)

@Composable
fun MyBottomNav() {
    val state = rememberGooeyNavIndicatorState(selectedIndex = 0)

    GooeyNavIndicatorHost(
        state = state,
        color = tabs[state.selectedIndex].color,
        modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
    ) {
        NavigationBar {
            tabs.forEachIndexed { index, tab ->
                NavigationBarItem(
                    modifier = Modifier.gooeyNavItem(state, index),
                    selected = state.selectedIndex == index,
                    onClick = { state.select(index) },
                    icon = { /* see "Changing the icons" below */ },
                    label = { Text(tab.label) },
                    colors = NavigationBarItemDefaults.colors(indicatorColor = Color.Transparent),
                )
            }
        }
    }
}

Three moving parts, always used together:

  1. rememberGooeyNavIndicatorState(selectedIndex) — one state object per nav bar.
  2. Modifier.gooeyNavItem(state, index) — on every item, so the state knows where it sits.
  3. GooeyNavIndicatorHost(state, color) { ... } — wraps the nav bar and draws the pill behind it.

Setting indicatorColor = Color.Transparent on NavigationBarItemDefaults.colors(...) is important: it stops Material's own pill from drawing on top of the gooey one.

docs.title: How the state works
docs.text:
If you're new to this kind of "shared animated state" pattern, here's what happens under the hood:

  1. rememberGooeyNavIndicatorState creates a GooeyNavIndicatorState and remembers it across recompositions. It does not track selection by itself — it only reacts when you tell it to.
  2. Each item's Modifier.gooeyNavItem(state, index) reports that item's on-screen position and size back to the state the moment it's laid out (via onGloballyPositioned). This is how the state knows where tab 0, 1, 2... actually are, without you hardcoding any coordinates.
  3. Nothing is drawn until at least one item has reported its bounds — so don't worry if the pill is invisible for a single frame on first composition; that's expected and happens before the user can see it.
  4. You call state.select(index) from each item's onClick. The host never selects on its own — this keeps GooeyNavIndicatorState a plain source of truth you can also drive from elsewhere (e.g. a ViewModel-driven LaunchedEffect).
  5. select(index) snapshots wherever the pill currently is (even mid-animation, if you tap twice quickly) as the animation's starting point, then animates to the new item's bounds using animationSpec. This is why rapid taps feel fluid instead of janky or queued.
  6. GooeyNavIndicatorHost reads state.selectedIndex and the live animation progress every frame to build the blob shapes, and draws them on a Canvas placed behind your content (the real NavigationBar), which is why your icons and ripples still render normally on top.

In short: the state is just data + an animation; your UI decides when select() is called. That also means you can trigger a selection change from anywhere you have a reference to state, not only from inside the nav bar — useful for things like deep links or a "jump to tab" button.

docs.title: Customizing the color
docs.text:
color is a plain androidx.compose.ui.graphics.Color — there's no special color API to learn.

// A fixed brand color
GooeyNavIndicatorHost(state = state, color = Color(0xFF6750A4)) { /* ... */ }

// Wired to your Material theme
GooeyNavIndicatorHost(state = state, color = MaterialTheme.colorScheme.primary) { /* ... */ }

// A different color per tab, swapping as selection changes (as in the Quick start above)
GooeyNavIndicatorHost(state = state, color = tabs[state.selectedIndex].color) { /* ... */ }

Because color is read on every frame the scene is built, passing an expression like tabs[state.selectedIndex].color is enough to get the pill to recolor itself as it slides — no extra animation code needed. If you want the color itself to crossfade (rather than snap) while the pill moves, animate it yourself and pass the animated value in:

val animatedColor by animateColorAsState(tabs[state.selectedIndex].color)
GooeyNavIndicatorHost(state = state, color = animatedColor) { /* ... */ }

docs.title: Changing the icons
docs.text:
There's no dedicated "icon" parameter — icon is just the normal @Composable content slot that NavigationBarItem already exposes, so anything you'd normally put there works, including swapping the icon per selection state:

import androidx.compose.material.icons.Icons
import androidx.compose.material.icons.filled.Home
import androidx.compose.material.icons.outlined.Home
import androidx.compose.material3.Icon

NavigationBarItem(
    modifier = Modifier.gooeyNavItem(state, index),
    selected = state.selectedIndex == index,
    onClick = { state.select(index) },
    icon = {
        val selected = state.selectedIndex == index
        Icon(
            imageVector = if (selected) Icons.Filled.Home else Icons.Outlined.Home,
            contentDescription = tab.label,
        )
    },
    label = { Text(tab.label) },
)

Reactify doesn't ship an icon set itself, so add one to your own app module (not the reactify dependency) if you don't already have vector icons:

// Compose Multiplatform (Android + iOS)
commonMain.dependencies {
    implementation("org.jetbrains.compose.material:material-icons-extended:<compose-version>")
}

// Android-only app
implementation("androidx.compose.material:material-icons-extended")

Emoji Text, your own vector drawables, or an Image with a bitmap/SVG painter all work just as well — the gooey pill only cares about the bounds reported by gooeyNavItem, not what's drawn inside them.

docs.title: Parameters reference
docs.text:
rememberGooeyNavIndicatorState

Parameter Default Description selectedIndex — Index selected the first time this state is created. Changing it on a later recomposition has no effect — use state.select(index) instead. animationSpec tween(450ms, LinearEasing) Drives the transition progress (0→1) each time select is called.

GooeyNavIndicatorHost

Parameter Default Description state — The GooeyNavIndicatorState created above. color — Fill color of the pill. Any Color, static or computed. cornerRadius null Corner radius of the pill. null draws a stadium shape (half the item's height) — the right choice for most pill-shaped indicators. smoothness 18.dp How far the gooey blend reaches; higher values make the bridge between old and new position wider/softer. renderer GooeyRenderers.auto() See Choosing a Renderer.

Modifier.gooeyNavItem(state, index) — no parameters beyond the state/index; apply it to the same composable that receives selected/onClick (e.g. NavigationBarItem).

docs.title: Tips & troubleshooting
docs.text:
The pill doesn't show up at all

Make sure every tab has Modifier.gooeyNavItem(state, index) applied, and that index matches the selectedIndex you pass to rememberGooeyNavIndicatorState. The pill stays invisible until the item at the initial selectedIndex has reported its bounds at least once.

Selecting a tab doesn't move the pill

state.select(index) must be called from onClick yourself — the host doesn't observe selected on NavigationBarItem. If you drive selection from elsewhere (e.g. a shared NavController), call state.select(index) wherever that selection changes.

There's a double pill

Pass indicatorColor = Color.Transparent to NavigationBarItemDefaults.colors(...) so Material's built-in selection pill doesn't draw underneath yours.

docs.title: Progress Indicators
docs.text: Liquid progress bars and rings. The determinate variants have a round head that races ahead when the value jumps, stretching a thin neck behind it that the fill then catches up with and absorbs; the indeterminate variants are drops chasing each other, merging and pinching apart as the gap between them changes.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
These snippets are self-contained; paste them into a @Composable and they run as-is.

import androidx.compose.foundation.layout.fillMaxWidth
import androidx.compose.material3.Button
import androidx.compose.material3.Text
import androidx.compose.runtime.getValue
import androidx.compose.runtime.mutableFloatStateOf
import androidx.compose.runtime.remember
import androidx.compose.runtime.setValue
import androidx.compose.ui.graphics.Color
import com.veroanggra.reactify.progress.GooeyLinearProgress

@Composable
fun Upload() {
    var progress by remember { mutableFloatStateOf(0f) }

    GooeyLinearProgress(
        progress = progress,
        color = Color(0xFFC8F5D4),
        modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth(),
    )
    Button(onClick = { progress += 0.25f }) { Text("Next chunk") }
}

Leave progress out and you get the indeterminate version; the same two shapes exist as rings:

import com.veroanggra.reactify.progress.GooeyCircularProgress

GooeyLinearProgress(color = Color(0xFFC4E4F7), modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth())

GooeyCircularProgress(progress = progress, color = Color(0xFFC8F5D4))
GooeyCircularProgress(color = Color(0xFFC4E4F7))

There is no state object to create: pass the value in, and every change animates from wherever the indicator currently is — tapping "Next chunk" twice quickly retargets mid-flight instead of queueing.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Two animations, one value. The determinate composables animate progress twice: a fast headSpec moves the round head, a slower fillSpec moves the fill behind it. While the two disagree, a chain of capsules joins them, thinnest in the middle in proportion to how far the head has pulled away. When the fill arrives the chain sits inside it and the blend hides it.
  2. One colour per scene. Everything gooey — fill, neck, head — shares color, so all renderers merge it the same way. The track is not part of the scene: it is a plain rounded rect (or ring) in trackColor drawn underneath, which is why it never bulges towards the head.
  3. The head fits inside the bounds. The head is 1.25× as thick as the track, so the track is inset: a height of 12.dp gives a 9.6.dp track with the head's overhang above and below. Set height to the total you want to reserve, not the bar thickness.
  4. Indeterminate loops are seamless. The linear sweep grows in at the start of its cycle and shrinks away at the end; the ring's three drops orbit one, two and three times per cycle, so the last frame of one cycle is the first frame of the next.
  5. Shader-safe blob counts. A full ring is sixteen capsules plus up to six neck segments and the head, inside the 24-blob limit of the AGSL and SkSL renderers; the CPU renderer has no limit.

docs.title: Parameters reference
docs.text:
GooeyLinearProgress — both overloads share every parameter except progress.

Parameter Default Description progress — (omit for indeterminate) Fraction done, clamped to 0..1. color — Fill and head colour. modifier Modifier Width comes from here (fillMaxWidth(), width(…)); without a constraint the bar is 240.dp wide. trackColor color.copy(alpha = 0.15f) Plain track drawn under the liquid. Pass Color.Transparent for none. height 12.dp Total height, head included. smoothness 10.dp Blend distance between head, neck and fill. renderer GooeyRenderers.auto() See Choosing a Renderer.

GooeyCircularProgress

Parameter Default Description progress — (omit for indeterminate) Fraction of a turn, clockwise from 12 o'clock. color — Arc and head colour. size 48.dp Outer diameter, head included. strokeWidth 6.dp Ring thickness; the head is 1.25× as wide. trackColor color.copy(alpha = 0.15f) Plain ring drawn under the liquid. smoothness 10.dp Blend distance. renderer GooeyRenderers.auto() See Choosing a Renderer.

GooeyProgressDefaults exposes headSpec and fillSpec for reference; to change the feel, drive your own animateFloatAsState values and feed the result to progress — the head/fill split still applies on top of whatever curve you supply.

docs.title: Tips & troubleshooting
docs.text:
The head is clipped at the ends

The indicator draws only inside its own bounds. Keep height (or size) as the total you want, rather than shrinking it to the track thickness and letting the head hang out.

No neck appears when the value changes

Small steps (a few percent) keep head and fill close enough that smoothness blends them into one drop. The stretch is proportional to the jump — try 25% steps, or lower smoothness.

The bar is 240.dp wide

That is the fallback width; pass Modifier.fillMaxWidth() or an explicit width(…).

docs.title: Pull to Refresh
docs.text: A drop of liquid that stretches out of the top edge as you pull a list down, hangs from a neck that thins the further you go, snaps free when you pass the threshold, and spins a small satellite while your refresh runs. It wraps any scrollable content — a LazyColumn, a Column with verticalScroll, a grid — and you keep full control of when refreshing starts and ends.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
This snippet is self-contained; paste it into a @Composable screen and it runs as-is.

import androidx.compose.foundation.layout.fillMaxSize
import androidx.compose.foundation.lazy.LazyColumn
import androidx.compose.foundation.lazy.items
import androidx.compose.material3.Text
import androidx.compose.runtime.LaunchedEffect
import androidx.compose.ui.graphics.Color
import com.veroanggra.reactify.refresh.GooeyPullToRefresh
import com.veroanggra.reactify.refresh.rememberGooeyPullToRefreshState
import kotlinx.coroutines.delay

@Composable
fun Inbox() {
    val state = rememberGooeyPullToRefreshState()
    var isRefreshing by remember { mutableStateOf(false) }
    var messages by remember { mutableStateOf(List(20) { "Message ${it + 1}" }) }

    LaunchedEffect(isRefreshing) {
        if (!isRefreshing) return@LaunchedEffect
        delay(1500)                              // your real fetch goes here
        messages = listOf("New message") + messages
        isRefreshing = false                     // the drop melts away
    }

    GooeyPullToRefresh(
        state = state,
        isRefreshing = isRefreshing,
        onRefresh = { isRefreshing = true },
        color = Color(0xFFC4E4F7),
        modifier = Modifier.fillMaxSize(),
    ) {
        LazyColumn(Modifier.fillMaxSize()) {
            items(messages) { Text(it) }
        }
    }
}

Three moving parts, always used together:

  1. rememberGooeyPullToRefreshState() — one state object per pull-to-refresh area.
  2. isRefreshing / onRefresh — you own the boolean. onRefresh fires once when the pull is released past the threshold; flip isRefreshing to true there and back to false when done.
  3. GooeyPullToRefresh(state, ...) { ... } — wraps your scrollable content and draws the drop on top of it.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The pull comes from nested scrolling, not from a gesture detector of its own:

  1. GooeyPullToRefresh attaches a NestedScrollConnection to the box around your content. When the content is already at its top and the user keeps dragging down, that leftover scroll is handed to the connection, which turns it into pull distance (with some resistance, so the drop moves at half the finger's speed).
  2. Dragging back up shrinks the pull first, before the content scrolls again.
  3. On release, the connection looks at how far the drop was pulled. Past threshold, the neck snaps, the drop settles at the threshold and onRefresh is called. Short of it, the drop is drawn back into the edge.
  4. While isRefreshing is true the drop stays put with a satellite orbiting it. When it turns false the drop shrinks to nothing and the state resets, ready for the next pull.

Because the pull is driven by scroll that your content couldn't consume, the content must be scrollable. A plain Column without verticalScroll never produces nested-scroll events, so the drop will never appear. The content itself stays in place — the indicator overlays it rather than pushing it down.

The state exposes pullProgress (pull as a fraction of the threshold, over 1 while over-pulled) and isRefreshing, in case you want to fade in a hint or dim the list while pulling.

docs.title: Customizing the look
docs.text:
GooeyPullToRefresh(
    state = state,
    isRefreshing = isRefreshing,
    onRefresh = { isRefreshing = true },
    color = MaterialTheme.colorScheme.primary,
    threshold = 96.dp,     // pull further before it triggers
    dropRadius = 18.dp,    // a bigger drop
    smoothness = 20.dp,    // a softer, wider neck
) { /* ... */ }

The drop can be pulled a little past threshold with increasing resistance; it never travels more than about 15% beyond it, so a long drag doesn't leave the drop dangling in the middle of the screen.

docs.title: Parameters reference
docs.text:
rememberGooeyPullToRefreshState — no parameters. Returns a GooeyPullToRefreshState with:

Property Description pullProgress Current pull as a fraction of threshold. 0 at rest, 1 at the threshold, above 1 while over-pulled. isRefreshing true from the moment the pull is released past the threshold until you set the host's isRefreshing back to false.

GooeyPullToRefresh

Parameter Default Description state — The GooeyPullToRefreshState created above. isRefreshing — Whether your refresh is running. Set it to true from onRefresh, false when done. onRefresh — Called once when a pull is released past threshold. color — Fill color of the lip, neck and drop. Any Color, static or computed. threshold 72.dp Pull distance that triggers a refresh on release. dropRadius 14.dp Radius of the drop. The neck and the lip scale with it. smoothness 16.dp How far the gooey blend reaches between lip, neck and drop. renderer GooeyRenderers.auto() See Choosing a Renderer.

docs.title: Tips & troubleshooting
docs.text:
Nothing happens when I pull

The content inside GooeyPullToRefresh has to be scrollable. Wrap a static Column in Modifier.verticalScroll(rememberScrollState()), or use LazyColumn/LazyVerticalGrid.

The drop snaps but my data doesn't reload

onRefresh only tells you the user asked for a refresh — it doesn't run anything. Set isRefreshing = true there and do the work in a LaunchedEffect(isRefreshing) (or your ViewModel), then set it back to false.

The drop never goes away

The drop melts only when the isRefreshing you pass in turns false. If your fetch can fail, make sure the error path resets it too.

Starting a refresh programmatically

Passing isRefreshing = true without a pull (e.g. on first load) animates the drop down to the threshold on its own; the user sees the same spinning drop as after a pull.

docs.title: Choosing a Renderer
docs.text:
GooeyRenderers.auto()   // AGSL on Android 33+, SkSL on iOS, CPU path tracing elsewhere
GooeyRenderers.path()   // force the CPU fallback
GooeyRenderers.plain()  // draw every blob independently, no merging — useful for debugging layouts

Pass the renderer explicitly to any host (GooeyTransferHost, GooeyNavIndicatorHost, GooeySegmentedControlHost) if you don't want the default.

docs.title: Sample App
docs.text:
The app module (Android) and iosApp (iOS, via samples-shared) both run the same demo: an invite-friends list, a bottom-nav indicator, and a segmented control, switchable from one screen.

samples-shared is a Kotlin Multiplatform module holding the demo's UI and state, consumed by both app (wrapped in an Android Activity) and iosApp (wrapped in a UIViewController via MainViewController()), so the demo logic and screens are written once and run natively on both platforms.

docs.title: Segmented Control
docs.text:
AndroidiOS

The same liquid pill as the bottom nav indicator, bridging between segmented control options as the selection changes. Use it for things like a day/week/month switcher or a filter row.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
This snippet is self-contained; paste it into a @Composable screen and it runs as-is.

import androidx.compose.foundation.background
import androidx.compose.foundation.clickable
import androidx.compose.foundation.layout.Row
import androidx.compose.foundation.layout.fillMaxWidth
import androidx.compose.foundation.layout.padding
import androidx.compose.foundation.shape.RoundedCornerShape
import androidx.compose.material3.Text
import androidx.compose.ui.Alignment
import androidx.compose.ui.Modifier
import androidx.compose.ui.draw.clip
import androidx.compose.ui.graphics.Color
import com.veroanggra.reactify.segment.GooeySegmentedControlHost
import com.veroanggra.reactify.segment.gooeySegmentItem
import com.veroanggra.reactify.segment.rememberGooeySegmentedControlState

private val options = listOf("Day", "Week", "Month")
private val Mint = Color(0xFFC8F5D4)

@Composable
fun MySegmentedControl() {
    val state = rememberGooeySegmentedControlState(selectedIndex = 0)

    GooeySegmentedControlHost(
        state = state,
        color = Mint,
        modifier = Modifier
            .fillMaxWidth()
            .background(Color.White.copy(alpha = 0.08f), RoundedCornerShape(percent = 50))
            .padding(4.dp),
    ) {
        Row(Modifier.fillMaxWidth()) {
            options.forEachIndexed { index, label ->
                val selected = state.selectedIndex == index
                Box(
                    Modifier
                        .weight(1f)
                        .gooeySegmentItem(state, index)
                        .clip(RoundedCornerShape(percent = 50))
                        .clickable { state.select(index) }
                        .padding(vertical = 10.dp),
                    contentAlignment = Alignment.Center,
                ) {
                    Text(label, color = if (selected) Color.Black else Color.White)
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

Three moving parts, always used together:

  1. rememberGooeySegmentedControlState(selectedIndex) — one state object per control.
  2. Modifier.gooeySegmentItem(state, index) — on every option, so the state knows where it sits.
  3. GooeySegmentedControlHost(state, color) { ... } — wraps the row and draws the thumb behind it.

The Modifier.background(...) on the host (the rounded, semi-transparent track above) is optional — it's what draws the pill-shaped groove the thumb slides inside.

docs.title: How the state works
docs.text:
This follows the exact same pattern as the nav indicator; if you've already read that page, skip ahead.

  1. rememberGooeySegmentedControlState creates a GooeySegmentedControlState and remembers it across recompositions. It only changes selection when you explicitly ask it to.
  2. Each option's Modifier.gooeySegmentItem(state, index) reports that option's live on-screen bounds back to the state via onGloballyPositioned, so the thumb always knows exactly where to animate to or from — including after layout changes like text reflow or window resize.
  3. Nothing is drawn until the option at the initial selectedIndex has reported its bounds once.
  4. You call state.select(index) from each option's onClick — the host never infers selection on its own. This keeps the state a plain, independently drivable source of truth.
  5. select(index) captures the thumb's current position (even mid-flight, if you tap again before the previous animation finished) and animates from there to the new option using animationSpec, so back-to-back taps feel continuous rather than queued.
  6. The host reads state.selectedIndex and the animation progress every frame to build the blob shapes and draws them on a Canvas behind your content, so your labels/icons and click ripples still render normally on top.

docs.title: Customizing the color
docs.text:
color is a plain androidx.compose.ui.graphics.Color:

// A fixed brand color
GooeySegmentedControlHost(state = state, color = Color(0xFF6750A4)) { /* ... */ }

// Wired to your Material theme
GooeySegmentedControlHost(state = state, color = MaterialTheme.colorScheme.primary) { /* ... */ }

// Crossfade the color itself while the thumb slides
val animatedColor by animateColorAsState(colorFor(state.selectedIndex))
GooeySegmentedControlHost(state = state, color = animatedColor) { /* ... */ }

Remember to also flip your label/icon color based on state.selectedIndex == index (as in the Quick start above), since the thumb only draws the background — it doesn't restyle your content.

docs.title: Changing the icons or labels
docs.text:
There's no dedicated "label" or "icon" parameter — the control's content lambda is a regular @Composable, so put whatever you want inside each option, including an icon instead of (or next to) text:

import androidx.compose.material.icons.Icons
import androidx.compose.material.icons.filled.List
import androidx.compose.material.icons.filled.ViewModule
import androidx.compose.material3.Icon

Row(Modifier.fillMaxWidth()) {
    listOf(Icons.Filled.List to "List", Icons.Filled.ViewModule to "Grid").forEachIndexed { index, (icon, label) ->
        val selected = state.selectedIndex == index
        Box(
            Modifier
                .weight(1f)
                .gooeySegmentItem(state, index)
                .clip(RoundedCornerShape(percent = 50))
                .clickable { state.select(index) }
                .padding(vertical = 10.dp),
            contentAlignment = Alignment.Center,
        ) {
            Icon(icon, contentDescription = label, tint = if (selected) Color.Black else Color.White)
        }
    }
}

Reactify doesn't ship an icon set — add one to your own app module if needed, e.g. org.jetbrains.compose.material:material-icons-extended for Compose Multiplatform, or androidx.compose.material:material-icons-extended for Android-only apps. Emoji Text, custom vector drawables, or images work the same way; the thumb only cares about the bounds reported by gooeySegmentItem, not what's drawn inside each option.

docs.title: Parameters reference
docs.text:
rememberGooeySegmentedControlState

Parameter Default Description selectedIndex — Index selected the first time this state is created. Use state.select(index) to change it later. animationSpec tween(400ms, LinearEasing) Drives the transition progress (0→1) each time select is called.

GooeySegmentedControlHost

Parameter Default Description state — The GooeySegmentedControlState created above. color — Fill color of the thumb. Any Color, static or computed. cornerRadius null Corner radius of the thumb. null draws a stadium shape (half the option's height). smoothness 14.dp How far the gooey blend reaches between the old and new thumb position. renderer GooeyRenderers.auto() See Choosing a Renderer.

Modifier.gooeySegmentItem(state, index) — apply it to the same composable that handles the click for that option.

docs.title: Tips & troubleshooting
docs.text:
The thumb doesn't show up at all

Every option needs Modifier.gooeySegmentItem(state, index), and the option at the initial selectedIndex must be composed and laid out at least once before the thumb appears.

Tapping an option doesn't move the thumb

Call state.select(index) yourself from that option's clickable {} — the host doesn't inspect your Row's children to detect taps.

The thumb is the wrong height

With cornerRadius = null (the default), the thumb's height comes from the option's own measured bounds, so give your options consistent padding if you want a uniform pill height.

docs.title: Stepper
docs.text: A liquid chain of dots that grows link by link as the user moves through a flow: a thread stretches from the current dot to the next one, thins in the middle like a drop being drawn out, then the new dot swells out of its tip. Going back plays the same picture in reverse. It wraps any row (or column) of step markers — you add one Modifier per marker and one state object.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
This snippet is self-contained; paste it into a @Composable screen and it runs as-is.

import androidx.compose.foundation.background
import androidx.compose.foundation.layout.Arrangement
import androidx.compose.foundation.layout.Box
import androidx.compose.foundation.layout.Row
import androidx.compose.foundation.layout.fillMaxWidth
import androidx.compose.foundation.layout.size
import androidx.compose.foundation.shape.CircleShape
import androidx.compose.material3.Button
import androidx.compose.material3.Text
import androidx.compose.ui.graphics.Color
import androidx.compose.ui.unit.dp
import com.veroanggra.reactify.stepper.GooeyStepperHost
import com.veroanggra.reactify.stepper.gooeyStep
import com.veroanggra.reactify.stepper.rememberGooeyStepperState

private val steps = listOf("Cart", "Address", "Payment", "Done")

@Composable
fun MyStepper() {
    val state = rememberGooeyStepperState(currentStep = 0)

    GooeyStepperHost(state = state, color = Color(0xFFFFD6A5), modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth()) {
        Row(Modifier.fillMaxWidth(), horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.SpaceBetween) {
            steps.forEachIndexed { index, _ ->
                Box(
                    Modifier
                        .size(28.dp)
                        .gooeyStep(state, index)
                        .background(Color.White.copy(alpha = 0.12f), CircleShape),
                )
            }
        }
    }

    Button(onClick = { state.next() }) { Text("Next") }
    Button(onClick = { state.previous() }) { Text("Previous") }
}

Three moving parts, always used together:

  1. rememberGooeyStepperState(currentStep) — one state object per stepper.
  2. Modifier.gooeyStep(state, index) — on every step marker, so the state knows where it sits.
  3. GooeyStepperHost(state, color) { ... } — wraps the markers and draws the chain behind them.

The host draws dots and links behind your content, so the markers themselves stay yours: a number, an icon, a check mark — anything. Give them a translucent or transparent background so the dot shows through.

docs.title: How the state works
docs.text:
1. rememberGooeyStepperState creates a GooeyStepperState and remembers it across recompositions. It never advances on its own — only next(), previous() and goTo(index) do.
  2. Each marker's Modifier.gooeyStep(state, index) reports its on-screen bounds to the state the moment it's laid out (via onGloballyPositioned). Indices must run contiguously from 0; the dot radius defaults to half the smallest marker.
  3. Nothing is drawn until the marker at the current step has reported its bounds — expect one invisible frame on first composition.
  4. goTo(index) (which next()/previous() call) sets currentStep immediately and starts the transition. Jumping several steps grows each link in order, one after the other.
  5. A tap during a transition retargets from the step the chain has visibly reached, so rapid taps feel fluid instead of queued.
  6. GooeyStepperHost reads the live progress every frame, builds the blobs and hands them to the renderer on a Canvas placed behind content.

docs.title: Customizing the look
docs.text:
color is a plain Color read every frame, so you can pass a theme color, a per-step color, or an animateColorAsState value. dotRadius sets the completed-dot size explicitly (by default it is derived from the marker size); smoothness controls how far the gooey blend reaches between the thread and the dots.

GooeyStepperHost(
    state = state,
    color = MaterialTheme.colorScheme.primary,
    dotRadius = 14.dp,
    smoothness = 18.dp,
) { /* ... */ }

docs.title: Parameters reference
docs.text:
rememberGooeyStepperState

Parameter Default Description currentStep — Step shown the first time this state is created. Changing it later has no effect — use goTo(index). animationSpec tween(450ms, LinearEasing) Drives the transition progress (0→1) for every step change.

GooeyStepperState

Member Description currentStep Index of the current step; updates as soon as a transition starts. stepCount Number of markers that have reported their bounds. goTo(index) Animates to index; ignored if that marker hasn't reported bounds. next() / previous() goTo(currentStep ± 1).

GooeyStepperHost

Parameter Default Description state — The GooeyStepperState created above. color — Fill color of the dots, links and thread. dotRadius null Radius of a completed dot. null uses half the smallest side of the step markers. smoothness 14.dp How far the gooey blend reaches between dot and thread. renderer GooeyRenderers.auto() See Choosing a Renderer.

Modifier.gooeyStep(state, index) — apply to each step marker; indices contiguous from 0.

docs.title: Tips & troubleshooting
docs.text:
Nothing is drawn

Every marker needs Modifier.gooeyStep(state, index), and the index you pass as currentStep must exist. The chain stays invisible until that marker has reported its bounds.

The dots look clipped

The host only draws inside its own bounds. If markers sit flush against the edge, add padding to the host so the dot and the gooey blend have room.

Vertical steppers

Lay the markers out in a Column instead of a Row — links follow the marker centers, so orientation doesn't matter.

docs.title: Transfer: list item → card
docs.text:
AndroidiOS

Wrap the screen in a GooeyTransferHost, mark each source row with GooeySource, and give the target card a GooeyTarget. Tapping (or long-press-dragging) a source transfers its token into the target, with a gooey bridge connecting the two while it travels.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
val state = rememberGooeyTransferState()

GooeyTransferHost(state = state) {
    Column {
        GooeyTarget(state = state, cornerRadius = 28.dp) {
            TransferredTokens()
        }

        LazyColumn {
            items(friends, key = { it.id }) { friend ->
                GooeySource(
                    state = state,
                    key = friend.id,
                    color = friend.tint,
                    cornerRadius = 16.dp,
                    token = { Avatar(friend) },
                ) {
                    FriendRow(friend, avatarModifier = Modifier.tokenAnchor())
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

tokenAnchor() marks where inside the row the flying copy visually starts from.

Four moving parts, always used together:

  1. rememberGooeyTransferState() — one state object per screen/host.
  2. GooeyTransferHost(state) { ... } — draws the gooey overlay and in-flight tokens above everything inside it; sources and targets can live anywhere inside, including inside a LazyColumn.
  3. GooeySource(state, key, color, token) { content } — a row/card whose token flies into the target when tapped (or dragged).
  4. GooeyTarget(state) { TransferredTokens() } — the destination; TransferredTokens() renders the row of tokens that have arrived.

docs.title: How the state works
docs.text:
GooeyTransferState is a bit more involved than the nav indicator / segmented control states, because it's coordinating several sources, one target, and (optionally) an in-progress drag — but the underlying idea is the same: the state only holds data and runs animations; your UI decides when things happen.

  1. rememberGooeyTransferState() creates one GooeyTransferState shared by every GooeySource and the GooeyTarget inside the same GooeyTransferHost.
  2. Every GooeySource registers itself with the state (keyed by the key you pass) as soon as it enters composition, and unregisters when it leaves — this is what makes it safe to put sources inside a LazyColumn: a row that's scrolled off-screen is simply not registered until it's recomposed again.
  3. Tapping a source calls state.transfer(key) internally (bound to .clickable for you) — you don't normally call this yourself unless you're triggering a transfer from somewhere other than a tap, e.g. a button elsewhere on screen.
  4. While a token is flying, it's tracked as a TransferredItem with its own progress animation. GooeyTransferHost reads every in-flight item's progress each frame to build the blob shapes (source blob, bridge, target blob) and to position the actual flying token composable on top.
  5. Once progress reaches 1f, the token "lands" — GooeyTarget's TransferredTokens() then draws it as a resting token in its row.
  6. Dragging (long-press and drag, enabled by default) runs a separate DragSession: the token follows your finger with a gooey "neck" stretching back to the source, and on release the state decides whether to commit the transfer or spring back, based on how close to the target you let go and how fast you were moving (FlingVelocity).

docs.title: State you can read and call yourself
docs.text:
Member What it does state.transfer(key) Starts (or resumes) moving a source's token into the target. Normally called for you by tapping a GooeySource. state.returnToSource(key) Animates a resting token back out of the target to its source, then removes it. Wired to tapping a token in TransferredTokens() when removable = true (the default). state.remove(key) Removes a token from the target instantly, with no animation — use this for things like "clear all" or restoring saved state without replaying the transfer. state.isTransferred(key) true once that key has landed in the target. Useful for dimming/disabling a source row (this already happens automatically — see below). state.transferredKeys The current target contents, newest first — read this to know what's "in the cart" right now. state.isAnimating true while anything (a drag or a flight) is in progress — handy to disable other interactions mid-animation.

Note that GooeySource already dims itself (transferredAlpha) and disables its own tap/drag once its key is transferred, using state.isTransferred(key) internally — you don't need to wire that up by hand.

docs.title: Customizing the colors
docs.text:
Each GooeySource has its own color — this is what makes a per-item tint possible (e.g. one color per friend, per product, per category), unlike the nav indicator/segmented control which take one shared color for the whole host:

GooeySource(
    state = state,
    key = friend.id,
    color = friend.tint,       // any androidx.compose.ui.graphics.Color, per item
    cornerRadius = 16.dp,
    token = { Avatar(friend) },
) { FriendRow(friend, avatarModifier = Modifier.tokenAnchor()) }

Two more parameters control how color is used, both on GooeyTransferHost:

  • maxTintAlpha (default 0.55f) — how strongly the bridge/blob tints toward color at its most intense point mid-flight. Lower it for a more subtle, mostly-white bridge.
  • On GooeySource, transferredAlpha (default 0.45f) — the opacity the source row fades to once its token has been transferred, so it reads as "already added" without disappearing.
GooeyTransferHost(state = state, maxTintAlpha = 0.3f) { /* ... */ }

A per-item color is also simplest way to make sure the flying token and the row it came from read as "the same object" — pick it from your data (as friend.tint does above) or from your theme, e.g. MaterialTheme.colorScheme.primary.

docs.title: Changing the token / icon
docs.text:
token is a plain @Composable () -> Unit — there's no special "icon" API. It's used in two places automatically: as the flying copy while in transit, and as the resting item inside TransferredTokens(). Swap it for anything of a similar aspect ratio — an avatar, a product thumbnail, an emoji, or a Material icon:

import androidx.compose.material.icons.Icons
import androidx.compose.material.icons.filled.Star
import androidx.compose.material3.Icon

GooeySource(
    state = state,
    key = product.id,
    color = product.tint,
    token = {
        Icon(
            imageVector = Icons.Filled.Star,
            contentDescription = product.name,
            tint = Color.Black,
        )
    },
) { ProductRow(product) }

Reactify doesn't ship icons itself — add org.jetbrains.compose.material:material-icons-extended (Compose Multiplatform) or androidx.compose.material:material-icons-extended (Android-only) to your own app module if you want Material icons instead of emoji/avatars.

Two details that matter when swapping token:

  • Whatever you put in token is measured at the source row's size the first time it's drawn, then scaled as it flies — so keep it roughly square (like an avatar or icon) rather than a wide piece of text, or it will stretch oddly mid-flight.
  • Modifier.tokenAnchor(), applied inside the source's content, marks exactly where the flying copy visually starts from (e.g. right on top of a small avatar inside a bigger row) — omit it and the whole row's bounds are used as the starting point instead.

TransferredTokens() itself (called inside GooeyTarget) takes its own styling parameters:

TransferredTokens(
    tokenSize = 32.dp,   // size each resting token is drawn at
    spacing = 6.dp,      // gap between resting tokens
    removable = true,    // tap a resting token to send it back to its source
)

docs.title: Pairing with a notch shape
docs.text:
Pair the target with a GooeyNotchShape to make the card's background open a matching notch as tokens arrive — this is what makes the card look like it's "swallowing" the token:

val notchRadius by animateDpAsState(if (collapsed) 30.dp else 0.dp)

GooeyTarget(
    state = state,
    cornerRadius = 28.dp,
    notchRadius = notchRadius,
    modifier = Modifier.background(CardYellow, GooeyNotchShape(cornerRadius = 28.dp, notchRadius = notchRadius)),
) {
    TransferredTokens()
}

notchRadius must be passed to both places — GooeyTarget (so the gooey overlay bends around the notch) and GooeyNotchShape (so the background actually has a matching concave cutout) — and cornerRadius must match between them too. Animate notchRadius yourself (as above, with animateDpAsState or a spring); the shape and overlay just follow whatever value you give them.

docs.title: Tap vs. drag
docs.text:
Both are enabled by default on every GooeySource:

  • Tap always transfers the token immediately.
  • Long-press, then drag picks the token up and follows your finger, stretching a gooey neck back to the source; releasing it near the target (or flinging it towards the target fast enough) commits the transfer, otherwise it springs back. The long-press requirement keeps this from fighting with scrolling in a LazyColumn.

Disable drag (keep tap-to-transfer only) with dragEnabled = false, or disable both interactions with enabled = false (e.g. while something else is loading).

docs.title: Parameters reference
docs.text:
rememberGooeyTransferState

Parameter Default Description animationSpec tween(1100ms, LinearEasing) Drives the master flight progress (0→1). Keep it linear — the grow/stretch/pinch shape itself is already baked into the choreography, not into easing.

GooeyTransferHost

Parameter Default Description state — The shared GooeyTransferState. renderer GooeyRenderers.auto() See Choosing a Renderer. smoothness 24.dp How far the gooey blend reaches around the bridge/blobs. maxTintAlpha 0.55f Maximum tint intensity of the bridge/blob toward the source's color.

GooeySource

Parameter Default Description key — Identifies this source; must be stable and unique (e.g. an id), same idea as LazyColumn's key. color — Tint for this source's gooey overlay. token — The flying/resting content — see "Changing the token / icon" above. cornerRadius 16.dp Must match the visual corner radius of content's background, or the blob won't line up with the row. enabled true Disables both tap and drag when false. dragEnabled true Disables long-press-drag while keeping tap-to-transfer. transferredAlpha 0.45f Opacity the row fades to once transferred.

GooeyTarget

Parameter Default Description cornerRadius 16.dp Must match the visual corner radius of content's background. notchRadius 0.dp Current radius of a paired GooeyNotchShape notch, if any — see "Pairing with a notch shape".

docs.title: Tips & troubleshooting
docs.text:
Tokens don't fly anywhere

GooeyTransferHost must be an ancestor of both the GooeySources and the GooeyTarget — it's the thing that actually draws the overlay. A GooeySource or GooeyTarget outside the host has nowhere to render into.

The flying token is squashed or stretched oddly

Give token a roughly square aspect ratio, and double-check cornerRadius on GooeySource / GooeyTarget matches the real corner radius of your row/card backgrounds — a mismatch here is the most common cause of the blob looking visually "off" from the content underneath it.

A transfer started before a row scrolled off-screen looks wrong when it lands

This is expected to self-correct: in-flight transfers re-read the source's live bounds each frame, so they follow the row while it's still composed; once it scrolls away, the last known bounds are used for the rest of the flight, and landing always targets the target's current bounds, which doesn't move.
